summary: A list changed in place needs .touch() and { equals: () => false } on list(), and then every row re-projects on every patch
detail: The rule (SKILL.md 9, when-list, realtime): mutate rows in place, then .touch(); a keyed list() over them needs { equals: () => false }. The trap: list() pushes each row with entry.item.set(arr[i]), gated by the row's equals; an in-place change re-delivers the same reference, which Object.is calls unchanged, so the row stays stale, silently. The workaround's cost: with equals: () => false every row's signal fires on every touch, because touch() carries no key and list() cannot tell which row changed. In the example (jobs.ts apply(): Object.assign(known, msg.job); jobs.touch(); jobs-view.tsx: list(shown, ..., { equals: () => false })) a JobRow has six projections, so one job's patch runs 6 x N of them (30,000 at JOBS=5000); the DOM stays minimal only because each bails on an unchanged primitive, which is why the row's style must be a string, not an object (the comment in JobRow). And in-place is three steps (peek, change, touch): a forgotten touch is another silent stale row. The API change that removes the rule: a keyed change list() can see, e.g. a keyed collection signal (collection<T>(key) with add / patch(key, fields) / remove, or touch(...keys)) that list() consumes per key, notifying only the changed rows' signals, whatever their equals. Then neither .touch() nor equals: () => false is written, and a patch costs the rows it changed.
note: 2026-10-20: found writing examples/jobs, railroad's worked example (Peter: a skill's rules are shown working in an example). The API is unchanged; Peter decides the change, the next session builds it. 2026-10-20: fixed: collection(key) (signals.ts) keeps rows by key, and put / patch / remove / set replace the row a change names with a new object and leave the others as they were, so list()'s per-row Object.is pushes on the changed row alone, over the collection or anything filtered or sorted from it; .get() is a fresh array per change. list()'s options argument is gone (Breaking): neither .touch() nor { equals: () => false } is written. examples/jobs: jobs.ts puts each job (no Object.assign, no touch), and webview-examples.test.ts asserts a patch to one job runs no other row's projections (the other rows read nothing) besides writing only that row's nodes. On Peter's word, 20 October.

summary: One row of a list changed in place is followed only by a projection with { equals: () => false }, which then wakes on every patch to any row
detail: The rule (realtime, signals): a projection that returns the same reference bails after .touch(); project to fresh values or pass { equals: () => false }. The trap: jobs.map((all) => all.find(...)) returns the same job after an in-place change, so a job's page and a toast would never see it change. The example's job(id) (jobs.ts) says equals: () => false, so JobLive (jobs-view.tsx) and each Toast (toast.tsx) re-project, with all their when() and .map()s downstream, on every patch to every job. Same root as #4: touch() says something changed in place, not what. The API change: the keyed collection of #4 gives a per-key signal (jobs.at(id): ReadonlySignal<T | null>) notified only when that key changes, so job(id) and its equals go.
note: 2026-10-20: found writing examples/jobs, railroad's worked example (Peter: a skill's rules are shown working in an example). The API is unchanged; Peter decides the change, the next session builds it. 2026-10-20: fixed: a collection's at(key) is a ReadonlySignal<T | null> told when that key's row changes and no other (null while there is none; made on first asking and kept, so a key removed and put again is followed again). examples/jobs: job(id) and its equals: () => false are gone; JobLive and each Toast follow jobs.at(id). summary: A keyed row is a signal, never destructured: every field is read as row$.map((r) => r.field)
detail:
The rule (SKILL.md 3, when-list): a keyed row is ReadonlySignal; derive with row$.map, never destructure. The trap: the render function's argument stands where the row would be, and in list()'s index form it is the row, so (job) => job.name reads once in one form and is right in the other; TypeScript catches ({ name }) on a keyed row only because a signal has no name, and job$.peek().name in a row goes stale silently. The ceremony it costs: JobRow (jobs-view.tsx) writes job$.map((j) => j.x) six times, RunnerPanel twice more. The API change that removes the rule: hand a keyed row as fields, each a signal (a proxy over the row signal whose properties are memoized .map()s: row.name is ReadonlySignal), so ({ name, status }) =>
  • {name} {status}
    • is correct; then only the index form passes raw values, and it could go (static lists are a plain .map()).
note:
2026-10-20: found writing examples/jobs, railroad's worked example (Peter: a skill's rules are shown working in an example). The API is unchanged; Peter decides the change, the next session builds it. 2026-10-20: fixed: a keyed list() row is its fields, each a memoized ReadonlySignal (Row: a proxy over the row's signal, each field a projection made on first read under the row's own scope and disposed with it), so ({ name, status }) =>
  • {name} {status}
    • is right; render's arguments are (row, index$, row$), the row's own signal third; a primitive row is its signal (Breaking: (row$) => row$.map((r) => r.x) is ({ x }) => x, or (_, i$, row$) => row$.map(...)). In development, row.get / .peek / .map on a row with no such field warns. examples/jobs: JobRow takes its row apart, no job$.map((j) => j.x). The index form stays, for static lists. On Peter's word, 20 October.

summary: An async component or route handler must resolve to a thunk, because a browser has no scope after an await
detail:
The rule (SKILL.md 8, async): return () =>
after the await; a bare Node is an error. The trap is the platform's: no AsyncContext, so nothing made after an await has an owner. The example writes it three times (JobPage, JobLog, NewJobPage in jobs-view.tsx), and NewJobPage moves its inject() into the thunk to keep it under a scope. The API change that removes the rule: a promise as a signal (resolved(promise): ReadonlySignal<{ value } | { error } | null>, or when() taking a promise), so an async view is a synchronous component: const d$ = resolved(detail(id)); return when(d$, (v$) => ..., () =>

loading

). The thunk contract and the fallback prop could then go; or wait for AsyncContext (TC39, stage 2), which would let railroad restore the scope itself.

summary: An unkeyed route handler's params are its first match's: read params$, or mark the route keyed
detail: The rule (SKILL.md 5, routes): a handler runs once per pattern, so ({ id }) => ... keeps the first id; read params$ or say { keyed: true, handler }. The trap: the handler's first argument is a plain object, which invites the destructuring the rule forbids, and it is right only when keyed. The example keys #/jobs/:id and reads params$ in the catch-all (app.tsx), both to dodge it. The API change that removes the rule: keyed by default, since a handler that takes params means them, with an opt-out ({ keyed: false } or { layout: true }) for the wildcard layouts that must stay mounted; or give an unkeyed handler params$ alone.

summary: What an effect run makes is disposed before its next run, silently: a computed kept from one run reads stale
detail: The rule (SKILL.md 6, scopes): what must outlive a run is made outside the effect body. In the example RunnerPanel (runners-view.tsx) makes its computed beside the effect, and says why. This is the ownership model, not a workaround, but the trap is silent: a disposed computed keeps its last value and get() returns it, so label ??= name.map(...) in an effect works once and then never updates. The API change that makes it loud rather than removing it: in development, a read of a computed disposed with the run that made it warns, naming that run (a production build drops it, as the other warnings).

summary: A custom root placed by hand is scoped(build), plus removing its nodes yourself: scoped()'s dispose leaves them, and mount() only appends
detail: The rule (scopes): a custom root is const { value, dispose } = scoped(() => build()). The example's toasts (toast.tsx) are built from a socket's handler, which is no scope, and go first in their host, so mount() (append only) will not do; dismissing one is dispose() and then value.parentNode?.removeChild(value), and a forgotten removal leaves a dead node in the page (a DocumentFragment's nodes are worse: they must be listed before it is placed). The API change: mount(target, render, { before }) placing the nodes where asked and removing them on dispose, as it does now at the end; then scoped() is for roots that are not nodes.

summary: loggedRequest takes (req: Request) => Response, so a Bun route's typed req.params and its server argument are lost
detail: Found writing the example's API: jobs-api.ts reads the id back with a cast (idOf: (req as BunRequest<"/api/jobs/:id">).params.id). loggedRequest's Handler is (req: Request) => Response | Promise<Response>, and the wrapper passes no second argument. The API change: generic over the request and the rest, loggedRequest<A extends [Request, ...unknown[]]>(tag, handler: (...args: A) => Response | Promise<Response>): (...args: A) => Promise<Response>, which keeps BunRequest<path> and the server, with no Bun type named in logger.ts.
note: 2026-10-20: found writing examples/jobs, railroad's worked example (Peter: a skill's rules are shown working in an example). The API is unchanged; Peter decides the change, the next session builds it. 2026-10-20: fixed: loggedRequest<A extends [Request, ...unknown[]]>(tag, handler: (...args: A) => Response | Promise<Response>): (...args: A) => Promise<Response> (logger.ts) passes the handler every argument it is given, so a handler typed (req: BunRequest<path>, server) keeps req.params and the server; logger.ts names no Bun type. examples/jobs: jobs-api.ts types each handler's request (BunRequest<"/api/jobs/:id">), and idOf and its cast are gone. TypeScript infers the arguments from the handler, not from where the wrapper is placed, so an inline handler in Bun.serve's routes still says its request's type. delta keeps a copy of the logger (src/server/logger.ts) with the old signature. On Peter's word, 20 October.

summary: A when() branch over an object still reads each field as v$.map((v) => v.x), where a keyed list() row is now its fields
detail: #6 made a keyed list() row its fields, each a signal, so a row is destructured. when()'s truthy branch still gets v$, one ReadonlySignal of the value, so a branch over one job (examples/jobs JobLive: when(jobs.at(id), (j$) => ...)) reads j$.map((j) => j.status), j$.map((j) => j.progress) and a style from j$: the repetition #6 removed from rows. Two shapes for the same thing. The change, if wanted: hand the branch the same Row<NonNullable<T>> (fields for an object, the signal for a primitive, v$ third or second), using list()'s rowOf. It is breaking for every when(x, (v$) => v$.map(...)) over an object (delta's, dzql's and the template's included), and when(count, (n$) => ...) over a number would not change.
